thread.title: Rich Rodriguez on regional conferences

author: Bob Hertzel For WV News
title: Rich Rodriguez on regional conferences
text:
MORGANTOWN, W. Va. — Maybe Rich Rodriguez really did miss his true calling, as a lot of people around here were suggesting back in 2007 after Pitt upset West Virginia in the Backyard Brawl when the Mountaineers needed only to win a game in which they were favored by 28.5 points to win and eventually Ohio State for the national championship.
Maybe he shouldn’t be a football coach but instead should become the first commissioner of college football.
On a day when he spoke openly about changes being needed to be made to the new pay-for-play system being worked out in the college game, one centered around revenue sharing with the players and NIL compensation, Rodriguez carried his thoughts a step further and suggested a complete restructuring of the Power 4 conference schedule that must have been designed by the airlines and hotels of the world, making such bad use of geography that had Christopher Columbus had it in his day, probably would have discovered South America, not North America.
As he began speaking of the disintegration of long-standing rivalries such as the Backyard Brawl and the Black Diamond rivalry with Virginia Tech, he decided he might as well drop a flea-flicker upon the entire system to tear it up and start over on a regional basis where East is East and West is West and Stanford or Cal aren’t members of the Atlantic Coast Conference.
“I’ve got my own opinions, and I’m not afraid to share my own opinions,” he said. “I love the Big 12, but it would be nice to have some regional — having us all come together. Here we all come together and shake hands and give each other a group hug and have an eastern regional and a north regional and a south regional and everybody share the money. There’s money for everybody; we all can get along, like 60 of us or so. I think that would be great.”
Why won’t that happen? Probably because it makes too much sense.
“Did anybody else say that? Probably not. They might be afraid,” Commis ... eh, Coach Rodriguez said. “I don’t care. I think that would be great. I’m going to put in my pitch right now. I’m not speaking for anybody other than Coach Rod, that he would love for all the Power Four teams to come together, shake hands, and let’s get the biggest TV package in the history of TV packages and we could have Pitt and Virginia Tech and Penn State and Maryland and Cincinnati and maybe Virginia and North Carolina, all those right there and our fans can drive to it.
“We’d have a rivalry every year and everybody makes money. Nobody gets fired. Players get good. Then this place will be packed again and we can have — this will be the — how would you call it, the Texas regional,” he continued.
“Wouldn’t that be fun? Can we put that together? I’ve got all the ADs out there shaking their head like I’m nuts. I’ve got more time — a lot more time behind me than ahead of me. I want to see us get this thing right before I leave.”
The truth is, Rodriguez is about 40 years late with his suggestion. Back in 1982 and 1983 no less a coaching icon than Penn State’s Joe Paterno began pushing for a powerhouse eastern football league.
At that time you had the Big Ten and the Pac 10 and the Southwest Conference and the SEC and the ACC but before the Big East took root as a basketball conference, Paterno set forth to gather Pitt and West Virginia and Penn State and Syracuse and Boston College and Virginia Tech, all eastern powers, together into a conference that could challenge those other conferences for prestige and dominance.
Paterno was aiming at putting the conference together, creating a huge TV deal considering the markets that would be involved, creating easier scheduling, satisfying the need for rivalries and being on equal footing with the other conferences.
“It would have been the premier conference in the country at the time,” then WVU AD Ed Pastilong said.
It was said that Pitt was the strongest opponent of the conference and that led to any deal falling through. Upset, Paterno surprised everyone and Penn State joined the Big Ten in 1991, driving the Big East to take in football members and begin playing the sport.
Perhaps now, however, the timing is right and it’s time to begin thinking in terms of regional, not national reach for conference re-igniting rivalries, cutting travel costs, putting Olympic sports in a far more affordable setting.
Can you imagine a 16-team Eastern football conference with West Virginia, Pitt, Penn State, Maryland, Virginia Tech, Virginia, Louisville, Syracuse, Boston College, Rutgers, Miami, UCF, South Florida and Army and Navy?
